questions.q: For an innovation to be successful, it must
options: be advertised effectively.
address the needs of users.
have a registered trademark.
be launched at an appropriate time.
questions.explanation: A successful innovation must meet a genuine user need, otherwise consumers see no reason to switch — the failure mode the episode flags with the Zune. Advertising, trademarks and timing are TEMPLE supports, but none can rescue a product that does not address a real need.

questions.q: Which combination of factors most influences the success of an innovation?
options: Social demand and cultural values
Product demand and social implications
Timing and appropriate marketing strategies
Ease of use and economical manufacturing processes
questions.explanation: Within TEMPLE, timing and marketing are the decisive levers: even a strong product fails if it enters an already-dominated market at the wrong moment. This is exactly the Section-one reasoning the episode drills — success rests on the innovation-success factors, not on a good design alone.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the nature of entrepreneurial activity?
options: It provides financial backing and technical support for a new product.
It provides inspiration and creativity in the development of a new product.
It takes responsibility for the creative and social aspects of a new product.
It assumes the responsibility, vision and economic support for a new product.
questions.explanation: The episode defines entrepreneurial activity as taking a creative idea and, bearing the risk, developing it into a viable venture and bringing it to market. The other options each capture only one slice — finance, creativity or social responsibility — not the full risk-bearing entrepreneurial role.

questions.q: Emerging technologies provide designers with unique opportunities to
options: develop products that are innovative.
develop products that guarantee increased sales.
design products that have a limited range of inbuilt applications.
design products using existing technologies that have proved to be successful.
questions.explanation: Emerging technologies — the 'E' in TEMPLE — open genuinely new possibilities, as 3-D printing and injection moulding did for the Flow Hive. They cannot guarantee sales, and relying on existing or limited applications is the opposite of using emerging technology.

questions.q: An innovation launches with a brilliant design and strong technology, but fails commercially because a competitor already dominates the market and consumers see no reason to switch. Which TEMPLE factor most explains the failure?
options: Era — the product was technologically out of date
Timing — it entered an already-dominated market at the wrong moment
Legal-economic — it infringed a competitor's patent
Emerging technologies — it lacked the technology to function
questions.explanation: The episode's Section-one example: the product failed not on design or technology, which were strong, but on timing — the Microsoft Zune against the iPod is the classic case. Marketing also plays a part, but timing is the headline TEMPLE factor when a strong product enters a saturated market.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes creativity from innovation?
options: Creativity is the successful sale of a product; innovation is its design
Creativity is the generation of new and original ideas; innovation is the successful development and implementation of a creative idea into a real product that is used
Creativity and innovation mean the same thing in design practice
Creativity is necessary and sufficient for innovation; the two always occur together
questions.explanation: The episode frames it as 'the idea' versus 'the idea delivered': creativity generates the original idea, innovation turns it into a used product. Creativity is necessary for innovation but not sufficient — a creative idea that is never implemented is not an innovation.

questions.q: From memory: what do the mnemonics TEMPLE, SIRRI and LESEE each stand for, and what type of question is each tool for?
keyPoints: TEMPLE — the six innovation-success factors: Timing, Emerging technologies, Marketing, Political, Legal-economic, Era. Use it for 'why did it succeed or fail'.

SIRRI — the ethical and environmental themes: Sustainable technologies, Intellectual property, the designer's Rights and Responsibilities, Responsibilities to society, Impact on Australian society. Use it to 'analyse the ethical and social implications'.
LESEE — the five implications of an emerging technology: Legal, Ethical, Social, Economic, Ecological. Use it to 'appraise an emerging technology'.
The essay engine ties them together: TEMPLE for the success, LESEE for the tech, SIRRI for the ethics, SPEEG and C-CWT for the context, then judge.
questions.explanation: If you recalled all three expansions and what each is used for, grade Good or Easy. The episode warns SIRRI and LESEE are the ones that slip — drill those.

questions.q: From memory: what is the headline trap that spans the whole HSC — the two different sets of 'factors' you must not confuse, and what does each set judge?
keyPoints: Do not confuse the eleven factors affecting design (H1.1, FFA EQ NEW LOAd) with the six factors affecting innovation success (H3.1, TEMPLE).
The design factors (function, aesthetics, ergonomics, etc.) judge whether the design itself is good.
TEMPLE (timing, marketing, legal climate, etc.) judges whether an innovation succeeds in the world.
A single paper can ask both, so when you see 'factors', check which set the question wants.
questions.explanation: If you separated the two sets and stated what each judges — design quality versus innovation success — grade Good or Easy. Reaching for TEMPLE keeps you from accidentally listing the design factors instead.

questions.q: Discuss how entrepreneurial activity can influence the success of a product like a tap turner.
questions.modelAnswer: Entrepreneurial activity can drive a product's success by supplying resources — time, business skills and economic backing — that enable effective market research, manufacturing and promotion. An entrepreneur's networks can promote a tap turner to appropriate niche markets such as senior-citizen organisations, occupational therapists and medical groups, while legal support (trademarks, patents, standards compliance) protects and strengthens the design. Conversely, entrepreneurial activity can also lead to failure if the resources or skills provided result in ineffective manufacturing processes or inappropriate materials that produce a product with minimal function. Overall the entrepreneur's enthusiasm, risk-taking and resource support are vital from the designer's vision through to the final market release.

criteria.descriptor: Identifies issues and provides points for AND/OR against how entrepreneurial activity can influence the success of a product
Provides characteristics and features of entrepreneurial activity that can influence the success of a product
Sketches in general terms and/or indicates the main features of entrepreneurial activity that can influence the success of a product
Recognises AND/OR names an aspect of entrepreneurial activity that may influence the success of a product

questions.explanation: This is the Section-two 'entrepreneurial activity' question the episode rehearses: define entrepreneurial activity, explain its influence with an example, and reference the supporting agencies (GASP-I — funders, patent offices, industry). The risk-bearing and the agencies are the marks.

questions.q:
The images show some examples of the application of emerging technologies: 3D printing (a medical prosthetic leg), biometrics (a security fingerprint scan), nanotechnology (a health smart watch) and a smart card (an Opal travel card).

Analyse the potential impact of emerging technologies on society.

Your answer will be assessed on how well you: demonstrate knowledge and understanding relevant to the question; communicate ideas and information using relevant examples; and present a sustained, logical and cohesive response.
questions.modelAnswer: Emerging technologies developed to meet real needs will continue to change and improve quality of life. 3D printing of a prosthetic leg produces a more aesthetically pleasing, customised replacement with a short concept-to-market lead time, improving the user's mobility, independence and self-esteem. Biometrics such as fingerprint scanning vastly improve security by identifying individuals, and will expand to DNA, eye and voice recognition to help create a safer world and reduce identity theft. Nanotechnology in smart watches enables compact, multifunction products with real-time data reporting, encouraging society to monitor and take responsibility for its own health and fitness. Smart cards like the Opal card make travel payment faster and more convenient and help shift towards a cashless society, though they raise concerns over personal data security and can disadvantage older or remote users with limited access to technology. Overall, acceptance of these technologies will keep growing out of need, making life easier, quicker and more convenient while bringing new security and equity implications that society must manage.

criteria.descriptor: Shows a comprehensive understanding of the potential impact of emerging technologies on society; draws out and relates implications of the potential impact; communicates using relevant examples; responds in a sustained, logical and cohesive manner
Explains the potential impact of emerging technologies on society; communicates using relevant examples; responds in a logical manner
Describes the potential impact of emerging technologies on society; may include a relevant example
Outlines the potential impact of emerging technologies including a link to society
Shows a limited understanding of emerging technologies

questions.explanation: This is the Section-three pay-off the episode builds toward. Run the essay engine: appraise each technology across the LESEE implications (legal, ethical, social, economic, ecological), weigh positives against risks such as data security and equity, and reach a clear balanced judgement — framework plus evidence plus judgement, never description.
